section_summary: This section centers on repeated offers from New Orleans to supply Japanese diplomatic code books, the State Department’s refusal, and its later discussion of whether to alert Japanese officials or refer the matter for prosecution. It also contains embassy reporting and press reactions to Herbert O. Yardley’s account of American codebreaking during the Washington Conference, followed by a separate report on French criticism of the book. The pages are filed out of chronological order and include duplicate memoranda and newspaper enclosures.

people.name: David A. Salmon
people.role: Chief of the Bureau of Indexes and Archives, later Chief of the Division of Communications and Records

people.name: E. S. Smith
people.role: New Orleans correspondent offering Japanese codes

people.name: Genichi Momose
people.role: Former chancellor of the Japanese Consulate in New Orleans; offered code-book photographs

people.name: Mr. Bannerman
people.role: State Department correspondent or investigator

people.name: Edwin L. Neville
people.role: Counselor of the U.S. Embassy in Tokyo

people.name: Herbert O. Yardley

people.name: Nagayasu Ikeda

people.name: Kijūrō Shidehara
people.role: Japanese foreign minister; formerly ambassador in Washington

people.name: Yasuya Uchida

people.name: Baron Hayashi
people.role: Japanese ambassador in London at the time of the Washington Conference

people.name: Tomosaburō Katō
people.role: Admiral and chief Japanese delegate to the Washington Conference

people.role: Acting U.S. secretary of state

subfiles.title: Smith offers photographs of Japanese Foreign Office codes
subfiles.about: Smith offers code photographs and directs Salmon to Momose in New Orleans.
subfiles.summary: Smith encloses photographs and says Momose can supply complete copies.

subfiles.title: Reply declining Japanese code offer
subfiles.about: The Department declines Smith’s offer.
subfiles.summary: Salmon says the Department is not interested in obtaining the code.

subfiles.title: Duplicate reply declining Japanese code offer
subfiles.about: A second copy records the same refusal.
subfiles.summary: The Department again states it is not interested in the Japanese code.

subfiles.title: Smith renews offer of Japanese ciphers
subfiles.about: Smith urges photographing Japanese consular ciphers.
subfiles.summary: Smith alleges Japanese efforts to obtain U.S. ciphers and offers Momose’s help.

subfiles.title: Salmon explains earlier replies
subfiles.about: Salmon explains why Smith may not have received a reply.
subfiles.summary: An earlier reply was undeliverable because Smith supplied no street address; the Department still declines.

subfiles.title: Smith sends another cipher photograph
subfiles.about: Smith sends a partial cipher photograph.
subfiles.summary: Smith submits another specimen and asks for consideration.

subfiles.title: New Orleans address inquiry
subfiles.about: An inquiry checks the New Orleans address supplied by Smith.
subfiles.summary: A Japanese resident is found at 1530 Broadway, but postal carriers do not know Smith.

subfiles.title: Smith alleges Japanese interest in U.S. ciphers
subfiles.about: Smith links Japanese interest in U.S. ciphers to China policy and disarmament talks.
subfiles.summary: He cites three cipher photographs and again directs Salmon to Momose.

subfiles.title: Smith urges use of Momose’s financial difficulties
subfiles.about: Smith presses the Department to approach Momose.
subfiles.summary: He says Momose controls consular ciphers and needs money after a long illness.

subfiles.title: Request for information on Momose
subfiles.about: The Division requests further information on the Japanese code seller.
subfiles.summary: The writer refers Bannerman to his March 27 memorandum and asks what can be learned.

subfiles.title: Momose offers Japanese code books
subfiles.about: Momose offers photographs, film, and access to Japanese diplomatic code books.
subfiles.summary: Momose claims Japanese officials seek U.S. codes and describes safeguards around their own books. He offers to help visiting U.S. representatives photograph confidential volumes in New Orleans.

subfiles.title: Embassy report on Japanese reaction to Yardley
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, for the U.S. ambassador in Tokyo
subfiles.about: The embassy reports Japanese press and political reactions to Yardley’s book.
subfiles.summary: Neville says disclosures about decoded Japanese telegrams caused a sensation and intensified criticism of Shidehara and Japanese security practices. He forwards translated statements and newspaper clippings.

subfiles.title: Tokyo Nichi Nichi article on decoded Japanese telegrams
subfiles.about: Japanese political, foreign ministry, army, and navy voices discuss Yardley’s disclosures.
subfiles.summary: The article records outrage at American codebreaking and sharper criticism of Japanese officials for failing to protect diplomatic traffic. It places particular responsibility on Shidehara and calls for precautions at future conferences.

subfiles.title: Japan Advertiser report on Yardley’s book
subfiles.about: The paper reports official interest in alleged decoding during the Washington Conference.
subfiles.summary: It recounts Yardley’s claim that decrypted Japanese instructions affected the naval ratio negotiations.

subfiles.title: Japan Chronicle report on Japanese defeat at Washington
subfiles.about: The clipping attributes Japan’s naval-ratio concession partly to American codebreaking.
subfiles.summary: It says decoded messages revealed Japan could accept a 60 percent capital-ship ratio.

subfiles.title: Japan Chronicle editorial on code decipherment
subfiles.about: The editorial criticizes systematic decipherment and Yardley’s disclosure.
subfiles.summary: It likens decoding conference messages to opening private letters.

subfiles.title: Osaka Mainichi report on Japanese secret codes
subfiles.about: The paper reports Yardley’s allegation that Washington read delegates’ coded cables.
subfiles.summary: It connects the allegation to Japan’s naval concession and concern over the coming Geneva conference.

subfiles.title: Japan Times report on official reaction
subfiles.about: Japanese observers criticize Shidehara and the simplicity of Foreign Office codes.
subfiles.summary: The report quotes calls for stronger security at future conferences.

subfiles.title: Japan Times editorial, American Espionage
subfiles.about: An editorial reflects on espionage and the Washington naval settlement.
subfiles.summary: It treats code espionage as part of diplomacy and argues the decoded messages may have hastened agreement.

subfiles.title: State Department forwards embassy despatch to War Department
subfiles.about: Castle seeks War Department views on the Japanese reaction to Yardley.
subfiles.summary: He forwards the Tokyo despatch confidentially and requests comment.

subfiles.title: Instruction to Forbes on Yardley developments
subfiles.about: The Department requests further reports from Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: Castle acknowledges despatch 284 and asks to be kept fully informed.

subfiles.title: War Department account of Yardley’s codebreaking office
subfiles.about: The War Department explains the origins, funding, and closure of Yardley’s New York office.
subfiles.summary: The letter describes the joint State–War codebreaking operation from 1919 to 1929, including funding and Yardley’s service. It says his manuscript was never submitted for War Department approval and that State benefited from decrypted messages after the war.

subfiles.title: Forbes reports further Japanese discussion of Yardley
subfiles.about: Forbes forwards articles on the Yardley disclosures.
subfiles.summary: He identifies the articles as likely wireless-company advocacy and says Yardley’s book remained widely discussed and commercially successful in Japan.

subfiles.title: International Contest on Communications
subfiles.about: A three-part series uses the Yardley affair to argue for wireless communications.
subfiles.summary: Shiraishi condemns interception of Japanese diplomatic cables while portraying it as an established practice. He compares cable and wireless interception, argues that specialized wireless equipment makes interception difficult, and presents cable traffic as vulnerable. The series appeared October 6–8, 1931.

subfiles.title: Smith’s earlier code-book offer
subfiles.about: Smith says a contact will provide Japanese code-book copies.
subfiles.summary: He gives the contact’s 1530 Broadway address in New Orleans.

subfiles.title: Smith identifies Momose
subfiles.about: Smith directs Salmon to Momose for a Japanese consular code specimen.
subfiles.summary: Smith identifies Momose as consular chancellor and asks for a prompt decision.

subfiles.title: Woody offers Japanese phonetic telegraph code
subfiles.about: Woody offers an older Japanese phonetic telegraph code.
subfiles.summary: He says a Japanese operator gave him the copy in Buenos Aires about ten years earlier.

subfiles.title: Reply to Woody
subfiles.about: The Department declines Woody’s code offer.
subfiles.summary: Salmon thanks Woody but says current codes and ciphers meet Department needs.

subfiles.title: Momose encloses Japanese newspaper cutting
subfiles.about: Momose uses Japanese press coverage to renew his code-book offer.
subfiles.summary: He says the cutting shows Japan’s anxiety about U.S. ciphers and invites a reply or visit.

subfiles.title: Decision note on Momose case
subfiles.about: Officials discuss handling Momose’s offer.
subfiles.summary: Castle agrees against raising it with the Japanese ambassador; a possible Justice referral remains under consideration.

subfiles.title: Routing memorandum to Castle
subfiles.about: The Division sends Castle the Momose file and proposed next steps.
subfiles.summary: It notes a possible conversation with the Japanese ambassador and possible legal referral.

subfiles.title: Warning against raising Momose case
subfiles.about: Salmon advises caution because of publicity surrounding The Black Chamber.
subfiles.summary: The writer urges Castle to consider Salmon’s objection before speaking with the Japanese ambassador.

subfiles.title: Background memorandum on Momose correspondence
subfiles.about: The memorandum reviews Momose’s identity, offers, and possible legal issues.
subfiles.summary: It traces correspondence under Smith’s name, Momose’s later letters, a 1928 diplomatic visa, and his absence from a 1931 Japanese service list. It raises possible impersonation charges and whether Japan should be informed amid the Yardley controversy.

subfiles.title: Copy of background memorandum on Momose
subfiles.about: A duplicate memorandum reviews Momose’s offer and legal questions.
subfiles.summary: It repeats the account of Smith’s letters, Momose’s identity, and possible impersonation proceedings.

subfiles.title: Second copy of background memorandum on Momose
subfiles.about: Another copy records the same Momose background review.
subfiles.summary: It repeats the proposed legal question and concern about publicity during the Yardley controversy.

subfiles.title: Statutory excerpt on impersonating foreign officials
subfiles.about: The excerpt states a penalty for fraudulent impersonation of foreign officials.
subfiles.summary: It reproduces Title VIII, section 2, cited in the Momose review.

subfiles.title: Salmon’s recommendation on Momose
subfiles.about: Salmon advises against initiating discussion of Momose with the Japanese ambassador.
subfiles.summary: He fears the approach would invite questions about Yardley’s disclosures and suggests leaving the correspondence alone unless Japan raises the issue.

subfiles.title: Recommendation to leave Momose papers with Salmon
subfiles.about: The Division recommends no action on Momose’s offer.
subfiles.summary: Metzger expects neither prosecution nor conviction on the available evidence.

subfiles.title: Consultations on possible Justice referral
subfiles.about: Officials weigh referring the Momose correspondence to Justice.
subfiles.summary: Metzger doubts prosecution or conviction; Salmon fears publicity. The memorandum recommends leaving the papers with Salmon.

subfiles.title: Procedure for requesting Attorney General opinions
subfiles.about: The excerpt describes supporting material required for formal legal opinions.
subfiles.summary: It specifies legal opinions and citations to accompany departmental requests.

subfiles.title: Copy of consultations on Justice referral
subfiles.about: A duplicate memorandum assesses prosecution and publicity risks.
subfiles.summary: It repeats the recommendation to leave Momose’s papers with Salmon.

subfiles.title: Copy of Attorney General opinion procedure
subfiles.about: A second copy states procedures for seeking Attorney General opinions.
subfiles.summary: It repeats the requirements for legal analysis and supporting references.

subfiles.title: Momose sends further code-book pictures
subfiles.about: Momose sends photographs and urges acquisition before his planned return to Japan.
subfiles.summary: He describes pictures of confidential cipher books and says he expects to return to Japan after a September consular conference in Washington.

subfiles.title: Fort-de-France report on French criticism of Yardley
subfiles.about: Robertson forwards a French article criticizing U.S. codebreaking and customs intelligence.
subfiles.summary: He summarizes L’Aurore’s claims about Yardley, alleged copying of French commercial records, and U.S. customs cases. He questions one translation and says the article appears to confuse informer rewards with bribes.

subfiles.title: Translation of Jean Bernard’s L’Aurore article
subfiles.about: Bernard condemns alleged American diplomatic and commercial espionage.
subfiles.summary: The article recounts claims from Yardley’s book about deciphered Allied telegrams and stolen cipher keys. It then alleges Americans obtained Paris merchants’ records to support customs prosecutions.

subfiles.title: L’Aurore newspaper enclosure
subfiles.about: The visible French newspaper pages discuss Martinique’s proposed public borrowing and works.
subfiles.summary: The clipping compares proposed loans, infrastructure spending, and Martinique’s finances.
